questions.question: What is debounce? What is throttle? When would you use each in a real product?
questions.answer:
Debounce: Delays execution until after a specified time of inactivity. Fires once after the user stops. Use for: search input, form validation, window resize handlers where you only care about the final state.

Throttle: Limits execution to at most once per time window, regardless of how many times it's triggered. Use for: scroll position tracking, mousemove, infinite scroll triggers, rate-limited API calls where you want regular updates.
questions.tip: Real-world examples score better than abstract definitions. Mention 'Google search suggestions' (debounce) and 'Twitter infinite scroll' (throttle).

questions.question: Implement debounce with both leading and trailing options.
questions.answer: Trailing (default): fires after the wait period ends. Leading: fires immediately on first call, then ignores calls for the wait period. Many implementations support both via options.
questions.tip: Lodash's _.debounce supports both — reading its source code is valuable interview prep.

questions.title: Debounce — how many API calls?
questions.explanation:
Answer: 1 time
Each call to search() resets the timer. 'a' at t=0 — timer set for t=300. 'ap' at t=50 — timer reset for t=350. 'app' at t=100 — timer reset for t=400. After t=400ms with no new calls, callAPI fires once with 'app'. This is the debounce contract: fire only after the user stops.

questions.title: Throttle — how many API calls?
questions.explanation:
Answer: ~2-3 times (depends on implementation)
With leading-edge throttle: t=0 fires (next allowed: t=200). t=50,100,150 are dropped. t=200 fires (next allowed: t=400). t=250 is dropped. The key insight: it's far fewer than 6. Throttle rate-limits to max 1 per window.

questions.title: Debounce — closure variable check
questions.explanation:
Output: 3 (after 100ms)
d(1) sets timer → cleared by d(2) → cleared by d(3). Only the last setTimeout survives. After 100ms of silence, fn(3) runs. timer is the closed-over variable that persists across all three calls — that's the mechanism that makes debounce work.
